```{r}
## 23/24

plot(elite$height_cm, elite$PTS,
     pch = 16, col = "steelblue", cex = 1.3,
     xlab = "Height (cm)", ylab = "Points per game (PPG)",
     main = "Height vs PPG: Players Averaging 25+ PPG, 2023-24",
     xlim = range(elite$height_cm) + c(-8, 8),
     ylim = range(elite$PTS) + c(-1, 1))
abline(lm(PTS ~ height_cm, data = elite), col = "red", lwd = 2)
text(elite$height_cm, elite$PTS, labels = elite$PLAYER, pos = c(3, 1), cex = 0.7)

plot(nba$height_cm, nba$PTS,
     pch = 16, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.3),
     xlab = "Height (cm)", ylab = "Points per game (PPG)",
     main = "Height vs PPG: All Players, 2023-24")
abline(lm(PTS ~ height_cm, data = nba), col = "red", lwd = 2)

thresholds <- c(20, 25, 30)
data.frame(threshold = thresholds,
           players = sapply(thresholds, function(t) nrow(filter_elite(nba, threshold = t))))

# 1. The first graph represents the relationship between height vs and points per game. We have filtered out all the non-elite scorers (not averaging above 25ppg). This graph shows that there is a weak correlation between height and ppg. This year, taller players like Embiid, Doncic, and Giannis averaged higher points than shorter elite players. The clump of players around 25 ppg are all less than 190 cm, which shows that for this year there was a correlation. It must be noted that the line of best fit is influenced by a few strong outliers, Embiid, Luka, and Giannis are averaging much higher above the line than the rest of the group.

# 2. The second scatterplot shows the distribution of all players in the NBA. The line of best fit shows that there is not much of a correlation between height and ppg (it is almost flat). The fairly normal distribution in this shows that while there are a few outliers in the elite category, there are not any major outliers than influence the general nba too much. There is a very weak relationship between height and PPG in this visualization. 

# 3. The last calculation shows how many players are above 20 points, 25 points, and 30 points. This provides a perspective to why the elite players graph might look different from the general NBA, out of 500 players only 18 average above 25 points, which is heavily skewed by a few tall elite players that performed well over the season. As we look at other seasons, this might average out to reveal a very weak correlation between the two.
```

```{r Plots}
# --- NOTE: Make sure you ran the cm conversion code first! ---
# df$HT_cm must already exist in your dataframe.

# Plot 1: Scatterplot
plot(general_data$HT_cm, general_data$PTS,
     xlab = "Height (cm)", ylab = "Points per Game",
     main = "Height vs Scoring", pch = 19, col = "steelblue")
abline(lm(PTS ~ HT_cm, data = general_data), col = "red", lwd = 2)   # trend line
abline(h = 25, lty = 2)    


# Plot 2: Bar Chart (Average PPG)
general_data$Group_cm <- cut(general_data$HT_cm, 
                   breaks = c(0, 183, 190.5, 196, 203, 210, 300),
                   labels = c("<183", "183-190", "191-196", "197-203", "204-210", "210+"))

avg_cm <- tapply(general_data$PTS, general_data$Group_cm, mean)
barplot(avg_cm, col = "steelblue",
        main = "Average PPG by Height Group (cm)",
        ylab = "Average Points", las = 2)


# Plot 3: Boxplot (Scoring Spread)
boxplot(PTS ~ Group_cm, data = general_data, col = "lightblue",
        main = "Scoring Spread by Height (cm)", 
        ylab = "Points per Game", 
        xlab = "Height (cm)",
        las = 2)
abline(h = 25, lty = 2, col = "red")
```

```{r Analysis from plot 1-3}
#In plot 1, this graph plots every individual player Points Per Game(PPG), with a scattered line on the 25 mark showing the few players who got 25+ PPG. From the plot, the densest cluster of players is between 75 inches (6'3") and 80 inches (6'8").The red line is a linear regression line that represents the overall mathematical trend to the data. Since the red line is almost horizontal, it shows that there isn't any real relationship between Height and PPG.

#In plot 2, Although there is guide the difference in average PPG in those players under 6ft, the average PPG across the rest of the heights remain consistent, about 10-12. The low average of <6'0 players is also most likely due to there being small amount of players in the nba who fit that height, so the average is lower. Overall though, this plot shows that Height doesn't lead to massive difference in terms of PPG.

#In plot 3, between 6'0 and 7'00+, the median of PPG is very similar in between these height range. There are even some outliers in those groups who were able to score more than the rest. With the sole exception of those under 6'0, as they are rare, their data is very different.

#Overall, from all these 3 plots, there isn't any strong evidence that proves that height is a big factor in terms of a players ability in scoring, as there ranges of PPG were very similar in almost all the height groups. With the sole exception of those under6'0, however since they are rare, the data provided is limited.

```

```{r What is the number of players that have scored 25+ points per game?}
n_elite <- sum(general_data$PTS >= 25)
n_rest  <- sum(general_data$PTS <  25)

barplot(c(n_elite, n_rest),
        names.arg = c("25+ PPG", "Under 25"),
        col = c("firebrick", "steelblue"),
        main = "Players Scoring 25+ PPG vs Under 25",
        ylab = "Number of Players")
text(c(0.7, 1.9), c(n_elite, n_rest), labels = c(n_elite, n_rest), pos = 3)

elite <- table(general_data$Group[general_data$PTS >= 25])
barplot(elite, col = "firebrick",
        main = "Where the 25+ PPG Scorers Are",
        ylab = "Number of Elite Scorers", las = 2)
```
```{r Analysis of above}
# Only a small percentage of nba players can reach 25+ Points per game, and in that small percentage the majority of players who scored that much were in the heights of 6'3-6'5. However, no matter the height, anyone can become an elite scorer.
```
